title: How Your Phone Camera Takes a Photo

sections.name: Hook
lines: c_hook
Every photo you take is really several photos, stacked and blended by your phone in a split second.
c_title
Here's what happens when you tap the shutter, in five steps.

sections.name: Catching light
lines: c_lens
Step one. A tiny stack of lenses bends the light from the scene, and focuses it onto a sensor smaller than your fingernail.
c_sensor
That sensor is covered in millions of tiny light buckets, called photosites. One for every pixel.

sections.name: Light into numbers
lines: c_photons
Step two. Light hitting each bucket knocks electrons loose. The brighter the light, the more electrons collect.
c_numbers
The phone measures every bucket and turns it into a number. A photo is really just a giant grid of numbers.

sections.name: Adding colour
lines: c_bayer
Step three. The buckets only measure brightness, not colour. So each one sits under a tiny red, green or blue filter.
c_green
There are twice as many green ones, because our eyes are most sensitive to green.
c_demosaic
Then the phone estimates the full colour of every pixel, by looking at its neighbours.

sections.name: Stacking shots
lines: c_stack
Step four. Your phone is often already capturing frames before you even press the button.
c_hdr
It blends several of them, keeping detail in the bright sky and the dark shadows at the same time.
c_night
In the dark, night mode stacks many frames, averaging away the grainy noise that a tiny sensor makes.

sections.name: Finishing touches
lines: c_portrait
Step five. Portrait mode works out how far away everything is, then blurs the background, like a big camera lens.
c_finish
Finally, a processor fixes the colours, sharpens the edges, and squeezes it all into a small file. All in about a second.

sections.name: Recap
lines: w_recap
Lenses focus the light. Millions of buckets count it. Filters add the colour, and your phone stacks and polishes the result.
outro
So every snapshot is a little bit of science, and a lot of maths. Follow for more of the tech you use every day.
